intro: This is the Great Theatre of Miletus, 250 BC - 3rd century AD. Take a moment to feel its scale: it is one of the largest theatres in Anatolia, and its cavea, nearly 140 m across, opens like a stadium set against the hillside. Greek architects built it in 250-225 BC. Under Rome, in AD 68-96, it was rebuilt with a three-storey stone stage building, and that front survives, together with the workshops behind it, among the most complete anywhere.
spot-1: Now you are looking down at the orchestra, a half circle 27.34 m across. What you see here is the surviving mass of the Greek foundation of 250-225 BC — the ground on which the theatre's story begins.
spot-2: Now you are looking at the stage front. This is the three-storey Roman stage building of AD 68-96, and it survives together with the vaulted workshops that stand behind it.
spot-3: Now your eye follows the diazoma, the walkway that splits the seating in two. Count the rows if you like: thirty below it, twenty-six above.
spot-4: Now you are looking across the cavea. Eleven stairways cut the great bank of seats into wedges. And how many people could it hold? Its capacity is put between 14,800 and 18,500.
spot-5: Now you are looking at the upper gallery, the broad walkway that runs behind the top row. Here at Miletus the Roman cavea was tied to the slope by a supporting wall, binding the seating to the hill itself.
uncertainty: Finally, an honest word about what this model does not know. Only the two diameters and the capacity are cited; everything else is derivation. In a cavea nearly 140 m across, the row count varies between publications, so the model distributes 56 rows from the 27.34 m orchestra to the 69.9 m outer edge, at a 0.75 m tread, with a 1.8 m walkway in between. The height of the stage building, the depth of the stage, the eleven stairways and the columns lining the upper gallery are proportions read off photographs of the building. The velarium masts are not documented by excavation at Miletus; they are assumed. The model shows the Roman phase of AD 68-96, when the timber stage of the Greek foundation had long been replaced by the three-storey building — but the statuary that once adorned its front is not modelled.
